title: How Gas Helps Some Animals Float
summary:
Passing gas may make people giggle, but for some animals it has a useful job. Gas inside their bodies can help them stay afloat.

Florida manatees mainly eat seagrass, which is tough to digest. Tiny living things called microbes help break it down in the animals’ large guts. This process produces gas. Manatees can also swallow air.

Gas is less dense than water. Having more gas inside makes a manatee more buoyant, meaning it floats more easily. Its strong belly muscles and diaphragm, the muscle used in breathing, can squeeze gas in its intestines. Releasing some of that gas can help it dive deeper.

Sand tiger sharks use air in a different way. Many bony fish have a swim bladder, a gas-filled organ that helps them float. Sharks do not have swim bladders. Their oily livers help support them in the water, but many sharks keep swimming to avoid sinking.

Marine conservation biologist David Shiffman explains that a sand tiger shark can gulp air at the ocean’s surface and use it to hover in the water. He says these sharks have been observed releasing air through an opening called a cloaca, which also handles waste and reproduction.

Some turtles use their cloacas for another surprising purpose. They pump water into the opening, and oxygen from that water enters their blood. This is different from releasing gas.

An everyday bodily process can reveal some clever ways animals live underwater.
why_it_matters: These examples help explain how animal bodies work underwater and how gas can help animals float.
